results.draft_locus: Why Your Team Didn't Get Faster (Even Though You Did) ¶3
results.quote: Fred Brooks observed half a century ago that the communication paths in a team grow roughly with the *square* of its size, and that the genuinely hard work — integration, architectural decisions, untangling a subtle bug — sits on a critical path that does not parallelize.
results.finding: Flow reader 1, in the paragraph beginning “I did pause at this sentence in the team section”, reread because team size introduces a new variable into an argument about more output from the existing team; the connection to more changes and decisions arrives afterward. The section’s place and its additional-support function are sound, but making the existing team’s increased coordination load explicit before the Brooks comparison would remove this local interruption. Both readers accurately describe the post’s problem-to-action order, its prerequisite model/limits sequence, increasing scale, and evidence-led sections; neither requests section reordering. Flow reader 2 does not report this Brooks problem, so it is uncorroborated.

results.quote: It is whether you can *trust* what it generated — and trust is manufactured by the standards upstream of the AI, not by the AI.
results.finding: Flow reader 2, in the paragraph beginning “It Amplifies Quality — and Slop”, had to reread “standards upstream of the AI” because review and output filtering were just placed after generation; the distinction between preparing standards beforehand and applying checks afterward is stated explicitly only in the later Monday table. The order of sections is clear, and a local clarification of that timing would resolve the interruption without reordering. Flow reader 1 reports no such standards problem and says the quality section’s local explanation preserves the thread, so this point is uncorroborated.

The AC-1 reader explains that results depend on work, people, goals, standards, review, and the surrounding system; weak conditions can increase mistakes and maintenance. It uses the contrasting experienced-developer slowdown/perceived speedup and task-dependent correctness results as evidence of variation. It explicitly rejects multiplication as a prediction, notes new capability and nonconstant effects across user/task/context, and calls for comparisons with and without AI using distinct time, completed-work, correctness, and delivery measures. This meets every component of the expected answer without treating the arithmetic as a law.

The AC-2 reader identifies generation as a nonlimiting stage, explains that unchanged review capacity creates a queue while release throughput remains constrained, and follows the code through integration/testing/deployment. It also identifies added coordination and ownership work from larger volume, with possible higher costs and lower stability. This supplies the expected mechanism for unchanged delivery and increased ownership burden; the expected list of downstream stages is illustrative, not a requirement to repeat every label.

The AC-3 reader proposes a representative comparison with and without AI, separates time/tasks/correctness from felt speed, and follows stable delivered changes and downstream queues. It would locate and improve the actual limiting stage, strengthen goals, owner, context, structure, acceptance standards, evaluations, tests, and review, and budget for debugging, maintenance, and understanding before expanding. This directly meets measurement, downstream-burden, stronger-input, and constraint-before-scale expectations.
